title: Daily-mean water levels in 3,411 US wells did not step more often on earthquake dates than on placebo dates at any seismic energy density from 1990 to 2025
abstract: We tested if public USGS daily-mean groundwater levels step more often after earthquakes than on placebo dates. We used 4,031 wells (3,411 with a valid score; 14.2 million well-days, 1990-2025) and 47,064 ComCat earthquakes. We gave each well-day the seismic energy density e of the strongest event on that UTC day (Wang 2007 relation). A step is a robust z of 4 or more for the change between 5-day medians before and after the event. The placebo moves each event date by 30-400 days, with the same offset for all wells. The plan was fixed before analysis. Result: no e bin from 1e-8 to above 1e-2 J/m3 had a step excess after Holm correction. For e >= 1e-4 J/m3 (47,337 well-dates), 3.90% of well-dates stepped against 3.44% on placebo dates (95% range 2.47-4.65%, p = 0.20). The excess is -0.75 to +1.42 percentage points. Confined and unconfined wells, the |z| >= 3 threshold and a 30-day persistence test gave the same null. Post hoc, no single M >= 7 event date of 361 passed a false-discovery test. The largest responses after great teleseisms (Sumatra 2005, Iquique 2014, Haida Gwaii 2012, Tohoku 2011) were regional clusters of rises in northeastern states; the Haida Gwaii window contains Hurricane Sandy. Only near events (e >= 1e-3) showed a timing sign: 41% (95% CI 32-49%) of 201 steps had their largest daily change on the event days, against 28% for placebo steps. Main limitation: daily means detect only large steps (median threshold 0.28 m), so the test cannot see the small coseismic steps and oscillations that high-rate wells record. Network-scale earthquake-groundwater studies with daily data need precipitation controls or sub-daily records.

display.caption: Share of well-dates with a level step (|z| >= 4 left, |z| >= 3 right) on earthquake dates (blue) and on placebo dates (grey 95% range, dashed mean), by seismic energy density bin. n is the number of well-dates. No bin shows a step excess after Holm correction.

Post hoc test for each M >= 7 event date with at least 100 wells: step rate on the event date against the mean rate of the same wells on 2,000 shifted dates. Point size grows with magnitude. Labelled dates have the most responses; they are regional clusters (the Haida Gwaii window contains Hurricane Sandy). No date passes Benjamini-Hochberg q < 0.1 among 361 dates.

Post hoc timing test: the day of the largest one-day level change for step responses on earthquake dates (blue) and placebo dates (grey). An earthquake step must fall in the shaded days -1 to +1. Only the near-field set (e >= 1e-3) shows an excess.
